newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts see little hope for Ecuador reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts see little hope for Ecuador reforms.

text.p: Ecuador's political crisis has dimmed investors' hopes that the country will move forward with economic and structural reforms anytime soon, emerging market debt sources said on Friday.

"We should not expect much in terms of reforms. What happened here was that there was a backlash against reforms, and if (Fabian) Alarcon is able to consolidate his position over the next few days, he will move very carefully on reforms," said Tulio Vera, managing director at Bear Stearns.
Fabian Alarcon, the Speaker of Ecuador's Congress, was sworn in as president after lawmakers late Thursday voted to oust Abdala Bucaram on grounds of mental incompetency.
A state of emergency was declared on Friday as protests continued to grip the nation and Bucaram refused to step down.
Experts said the recent suspension of public sector tariff increases and subsidy cuts would most certainly remain in place.

"Alarcon is not likely to carry forward any of the reform policies that Bucaram had been pursuing. In fact, he is probably likely going to suspend them indefinitively, particularly the public sector tariff increases that Bucaram rolled back already," said Bill Romary, emerging market economist at UBS Securities in New York.
"It seems likely that he (Alarcon) will suspend them completely because that will appease the masses," Romary said.
"I think it is likely that there will be a significant backsliding in terms of reforms," added James Barrineau, Latin American strategist at Smith Barney.
On the fiscal side, economists said they did not expect to see the government make progress anytime soon.

"In terms of the country as a sovereign credit, I don't expect much improvement for the next year. The fiscal deficit will remain a source of problems," said Vera, who explained that the shortfall was a little less than 3.0 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP).
He said that represented a "significant deterioration" over the past two years as the country's accounts showed a surplus in 1994.
Vera said that Ecuador's fiscal balance last year should have been a lot healthier in light of its windfall oil profits.

"That was a windfall there, and that was essentially spent. So if anything, the fiscal accounts should have looked better last year and they looked a lot worse. So from a creditworthy perspective, the country deteriorated over the last two years," he said.
